cues.text: A Lawyer's Sudden Reversal
Born in 1696 near Naples to a family of the local nobility, Alphonsus Liguori showed precocious legal talent.
At only sixteen, he earned his doctorate in both civil and canon law, quickly establishing himself as one of Naples’s most promising young lawyers.
His legal career ended abruptly in 1723, when he discovered that he had overlooked a crucial document that would have won the case.

He discovered this only after the verdict had already been rendered against his client, a professional humiliation Alphonsus took to heart so deeply that he resolved, within days, to abandon the law entirely and pursue the priesthood instead.
Preaching to the Forgotten Poor

Ordained a priest in 1726, Alphonsus devoted himself to missionary preaching among the rural poor of the countryside surrounding Naples, a population he judged badly neglected by a Church more attentive to its wealthier urban parishes.
In 1732, he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer — the Redemptorists — a missionary order specifically dedicated to preaching missions among precisely this overlooked rural population.
A Middle Path in Moral Theology
Alphonsus's most enduring theological achievement was his monumental Moral Theology , composed and revised across decades of pastoral experience.

It charted a deliberate, carefully reasoned middle course between the excessive severity of Jansenist rigorism, which Alphonsus judged drove struggling souls to despair, and an opposite laxity that trivialized genuine sin.

This moderate, humane system would eventually be so widely adopted across the Catholic world that the Church has since held Alphonsus's own moral judgments as a safe and reliable guide for confessors.
A Reluctant Bishop
In 1762, already sixty-six and deeply reluctant to leave his missionary congregation, Alphonsus was compelled by papal command to accept appointment as Bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti.

He governed the small and troubled diocese for thirteen years with the same practical, reforming energy that had once distinguished his legal career — reorganizing the seminary, reforming lax convents, and insisting on serious theological formation for his clergy.
A Devotion to Mary Alongside Careful Theology
Beyond his moral theology, Alphonsus left the Church an extensive body of devotional and Marian writing, most notably The Glories of Mary .

He also composed hymns still sung in Italian Christmas tradition, showing that the same mind capable of careful, technical moral reasoning could write with genuine popular warmth and simplicity for ordinary believers.
Legacy
Alphonsus died at Nocera de' Pagani on 1 August 1787, at ninety-one years old, having spent his final hours in prayer before an image of Mary.
Canonized in 1839 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1871, Alphonsus Liguori remains recognized as the Church's foremost patron of moral theologians and confessors.

His single professional failure, taken as a providential sign rather than mere misfortune, redirected an entire career toward reshaping, with lasting and moderate wisdom, how the whole Church would come to understand and teach mercy in the confessional.
